metadata.title: eidos: A modular approach to external function integration in LLMs
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper presents eidos, a software tool designed to streamline the integration of functions within Large Language Models (LLMs). eidos acts as an intermediary, enabling both the seamless execution and validation of functions by LLMs.

sections.heading: Aldana-Montes
sections.text: ITIS Software, Edificio de Investigación Ada Byron, University of Málaga, Málaga, 29071, Spain Dept. de Lenguajes y Ciencias de la Computación, University of Málaga, Málaga, 29071, Spain A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Large Language Models Function calling Validation Retrieval-Augmented Generation A B S T R A C T Function calling allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute a wide range of tasks, from data analysis and mathematical computations to interacting with web services and other software systems. By harnessing the power of external tooling, LLMs can provide more dynamic, context-aware responses. However, errors in the model’s understanding of the request can lead to misinterpretations of the intended actions, resulting in function calls that are either irrelevant or incorrect for the task at hand. Without proper validation and control mechanisms, the parameters expected by the function may not align with those provided by the model, leading to incorrect operations or failures in task execution. In this paper, we present eidos , a software tool designed to streamline the integration of functions within LLMs. eidos acts as an intermediary, enabling both the seamless execution and validation of functions by LLMs. By leveraging its modular architecture, function definitions can be injected into the LLM context and invoked as if they were native functions via an API. sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: and significance Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT [ 1 ] have revolutionized the landscape of artificial intelligence by demonstrating remarkable proficiency in generating human-like text. These models have been de- ployed across many applications, from automated customer service [ 2 ] and content creation to more complex tasks such as coding and data analysis [ 3 , 4 ]. In this context, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [ 5 , 6 ] tech- niques have emerged as a powerful approach to create more dynamic, context-aware AI solutions. RAG models combine the strengths of LLMs and traditional information retrieval systems, allowing them to generate more accurate and contextually relevant responses. RAG allows LLMs to expand their utility beyond text generation, enabling ∗ Corresponding author at: ITIS Software, Edificio de Investigación Ada Byron, University of Málaga, Málaga, 29071, Spain. E-mail addresses: jfaldanam@uma.es (J.F. Aldana-Martín), antonio.b@uma.es (A. Benítez-Hidalgo), jfaldana@uma.es (J.F. Aldana-Montes). interaction with external databases, APIs, and software tools, enhancing their responses with real-time data and capabilities beyond their native knowledge base. However, the integration of external knowledge introduces new challenges. For example, hallucinations [ 7 ]—where models generate plausible but factually incorrect information—can hinder the extraction of user intentions for calling external functions or tools accurately. Hal- lucinating function names, and even argument names, when generating a function call can be problematic as it may led to errors in the retrieval process. Consequently, the dynamic nature of function calls demands a robust mechanism for validating the correctness of these operations. Table 1 summarizes the differences between e idos and existing tool use and orchestration frameworks. Although OpenAI’s native func- tion calling and LangChain offer basic support for tool use, e idos are designed with tool execution as a first-class abstraction, enabling more principled orchestration and grounding across heterogeneous tool chains and knowledge representations (e.g., combining formal ontologies with LLM). To the best of our knowledge, no existing work has focused on the development of a dedicated mechanism to streamline function calling and validation in the context of RAG. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this challenge. Our solution, denoted eidos , intro- duces a modular architecture that allows for seamless integration of function definitions into the LLM context. eidos automatically validates function signatures and outputs, ensuring that the interactions between LLMs and external tools are both meaningful and accurate. 2.

sections.heading: Software
sections.text: description 2.1. Software architecture eidos is a Python package with minimal external dependencies. The project is open-source and available on GitHub, 1 and includes a throughout testing suite, with a special focus on the validation module, and Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery pipelines for automated testing. eidos provides a completely modular architecture with two main components: validation and execution. The validation module is re- sponsible for ensuring that the input and output data is in the correct format and that the metadata is correctly defined. The execution mod- ule is responsible for running the user-defined functions and returning the results. The user-defined functions are expected to be in standard Python and are executed in the same environment as the main eidos process. Most functionality is provided through the REST API, which is built using FastAPI. It can be deployed as a standalone service (including serverless environments on AWS Lambda 2 ) or as a part of a larger application using the module directly (see Fig. 1 ). 1 In URL: https://github.com/KhaosResearch/eidos/ . 2 AWS Lambda: https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/ . To extend eidos , users need to implement their functions in Python and ensure these functions are accessible within the same execution environment as the main process. Afterwards, users must define the associated metadata in the specified JSON format, as shown below: def get_weather(q: str , units: str ) -> str : api_key = "your_api_key_here" base_url = "..." params = { ’q’ : q, ’appid’ : api_key, ’units’ : units } response = requests.get( base_url, params=params ) return response.text() Listing 1 Python function { "name" : "weather" , "description" : "Get weather information" , "module" : "weather.get_weather" , "parameters" : [ { "name" : "location" , "type" : "str" , "description" : "Place" , "options" : null, "regex" : null }, { "name" : "units" , "type" : "str" , "description" : "Units of meas." , "options" : [ "metric" , "imperial" ], "regex" : null }, ], "response" : { "msg" : "str" } } Listing 2 JSON representation To ease deployment, eidos provides a Docker image that includes all dependencies and can be run as a standalone service. It can be SoftwareX 31 (2025) 102290 2 J.F. Aldana-Martín et al. extended to include additional user-defined functions and metadata files as follows 3 : FROM ghcr.io/khaosresearch/eidos:v1.0.0 WORKDIR /app COPY app /app/weather COPY setup.py /app/setup.py COPY weather.json /functions/weather.json RUN pip install "." Listing 3 Example Dockerfile extending eidos 2.2. Software functionalities The main functionalities of eidos are as follows: • The execution of functions requested by LLMs follows the stan- dard format introduced by companies such as OpenAI and Mistral, while being extensible to new standards generated by the com- munity. eidos provides a generalized function definition format based on OpenAI’s specifications, designed to be easily extended to accommodate new definitions such as output validation. • Validation of inputs and outputs. eidos guarantees that the inputs generated by the LLMs are available on the same format as it was requested via the function definition through a combination of static checks and runtime validation hooks, which are defined declaratively in the specification of each tool. When the model produces arguments that deviate from the expected format or types, eidos employs a multi-tiered fallback strategy. This includes soft validation, where minor mismatches, such as safely coercing a string like ‘‘42’’ into an integer, are automatically corrected. If validation continues to fail after retries or correction attempts, the system resorts to a fail-safe rejection, returning a structured error trace that clearly outlines the issue. • Modular design without the need of a SDK. eidos is thought out to be easily extensible without knowing anything else than Python and JSON. • Cloud-native. eidos can be deployed i

sections.heading: Illustrative
sections.text: examples The following example demonstrates how eidos can be used to interact with a Geographic Information System (GIS) using an LLM. GIS and remote sensing are crucial tools in environmental monitoring, urban planning, and disaster management. However, extracting mean- ingful insights from vast amounts of spatial data requires sophisticated tools and expertise. eidos facilitates the integration of LLMs with these platforms, enabling users to interact with these complex systems using natural language queries. The first step is to define a function that retrieves the polygon of a parcel using a cadastral reference. The function definition includes the function name, input parameters, and output format, as shown in the following code snippet: { "name" : "geojson_from_cadastral_reference" , "description" : "Get the polygon of a parcel from a cadastral reference." , "module" : "eidos_gis.geojson_from_cadastral_reference" , "parameters" : [ { 3 A full example including an eidos client can be found at https://github. com/KhaosResearch/eidos/tree/master/examples/ . "name" : "cadastral_reference" , "type" : "str" , "description" : "Cadastral reference of the parcel." , "options" : null, "regex" : null } ], "response" : { "parcel_url" : "str" , "utm_zone" : "str" } } Listing 4 Example of a function to obtain the GeoJSON of a cadastral reference The actual function implementation is not shown here, but it is referenced in the module field of the function definition. The function is implemented in a Python module that must be accessible to the eidos server at runtime, i.e. the Python module must be installed on the same environment, and it returns a GeoJSON representation of the parcel and the UTM zone in which it is located allowing the user interface to render the parcel or the LLM to generate a response based on it. These function definitions are loaded by the eidos server at startup. eidos provides an endpoint that list all available functions, as well as their definitions and response formats, and another endpoint that executes a function based on the function name and input parameters, validating both the inputs and the outputs after execution. The LLM can interact with the eidos server using these endpoints, as shown in the following example using Python and the OpenAI client: import requests from openai import OpenAI tools = requests.get( "http://eidos-server/api/v1/functions" ).json() client = OpenAI() chat_completion = client.chat.completions.create( messages=[ # ...context... { "role" : "assitant" , "content" : "Is here anything specific you would like to know " + \ "about a particular plot?" , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "The cadastral reference of my plot is " + \ "14010A009000220000EE" , } ], model= "gpt-3.5-turbo" , tools=tools, ) Listing 5 Example sharing all available functions to an LLM using the OpenAI client In the aforementioned example, the agronomist can simply input a query referencing the relevant land plot, such as ‘‘The cadastral reference of my plot is 14010A009000220000EE’’. The LLM interprets this query and calls the appropriate function. The results, including the parcel and UTM zone, are returned and represented in the User Interface in a user-friendly format, as is showcased in Fig. 2 . Note that the function call is validated by eidos , ensuring that the inputs and outputs are consistent with the function definition. Little to no effort is required to set up this interaction. 4.

sections.heading: Impact
sections.text: Since the release of ChatGPT on November of 2022, LLMs have grow in popularity and have breach the barrier between research and general public availability. The potential of these models is still being explored, and the integration of external tools is a key aspect of their SoftwareX 31 (2025) 102290 3 J.F. Aldana-Martín et al. Fig. 2. eidos powering a chatbot with the capabilities of a geographic information system. The chatbot shows function calls and parameters during the conversation for debugging purposes. On the first answer, the chatbot provides the user the functionalities it has available from the functions defined in eidos and afterwards, a debug view of the function called and provided parameters is shown. After the execution of the function, the relevant geometry is loaded into the GIS on the left. development. In recent years, new Open Source models have been released and improved, including those with support for AI functions, such as all Mistral models [ 9 , 10 ], NexusRaven [ 11 ], ToolAlpaca [ 12 ] or Code Llama - Instruct [ 13 ], but there are still no platforms for validating and executing the functions called by the LLMs. The introduction of our proposed solution, eidos , significantly ad- vances this frontier by addressing a critical gap in the existing infras- tructure for LLMs. For users and developers, eidos changes their daily practice by simplifying the integration of LLMs with external tools. Its modular design and ease of use mean that developers can focus on building innovative applications in any domain without worrying about the complexities of managing function calls. For commercial settings, eidos is designed to be cloud-native and easily deployable in serverless environments. 5.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In this paper, we present eidos , a tool designed to streamline the integration and execution of external functions in the context of Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems. It pro- vides both RESTFUL API and a Python API, allowing users to integrate it into their existing pipelines. A key feature of eidos is its modular architecture. This design allows users to define and inject function definitions into the LLM context as if they were native functions, facilitating a smoother integration process. The use of a REST API further simplifies the integration process, making it suitable for deployment in various environments, including serverless architectures like AWS Lambda. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of eidos through a use case involving Geographic Information Systems, showcasing how the tool can support agricultural decision-making processes by providing a mechanism to ensure the quality of the output and the ability to execute functions in a secure and controlled manner via its API. In the future, we plan to extend eidos to support more complex func- tion definitions, including the ability to define function dependencies and execute functions in parallel. Finally, we plan to explore the use of eidos in other domains, such as healthcare and finance, to further demonstrate its utility and versatility. Collaborations with other open- source projects and contributions from the community will also be encouraged to continuously improve and adapt eidos to emerging needs.
